name: Bioresonance therapy

card.summary: A device-based alternative-health practice (MORA, BICOM) in which electrodes are said to detect and 'correct' body frequencies; practitioners offer it for skin conditions, allergies and hair concerns, which they say supports a clearer complexion and healthier hair.
card.note: Regulators and reviewers report no demonstrated mechanism; costs and delayed conventional care are documented concerns.

quick.overview:
Bioresonance therapy is a practice in which a device with electrodes is said to read electromagnetic oscillations from the body and feed back modified signals to restore balance. Practitioners offer it for allergies, skin problems such as eczema, addictions and general complaints. In an appearance context, proponents link it to clearer skin and healthier-looking hair via treating allergy or inflammation.

It was developed in Germany in 1977 by Franz Morell and Erich Rasche. Research classifies the proposed mechanism as lacking scientific explanation, and trials reviewed in the literature, including a 1997 trial in children with atopic dermatitis, found no effect beyond placebo.
quick.how: Sessions typically involve holding or touching electrodes connected to a machine while the practitioner runs programmes; some devices also measure skin resistance. Courses of several sessions are common.
quick.risks: The direct risk is low, since the sessions are non-invasive. Documented concerns are the cost, delayed or substituted conventional treatment, and regulatory action: the US FDA classifies devices that use resistance measurements to diagnose and treat disease as Class III and has acted against sellers making false health claims.

lead: Bioresonance therapy, also known as MORA therapy or BICOM, is an alternative-medicine practice in which a machine connected to the client by electrodes is said to detect electromagnetic oscillations from the body and return altered signals to correct disease-related patterns.[1]

In looks-related settings, practitioners and clinics offer it for skin conditions such as eczema and allergy-related problems, and some offer it for smoking or other habits. Proponents describe the aim as clearer skin and general wellbeing; there is no established appearance-specific protocol.[1]

Researchers describe the proposed mechanism as lacking a scientific explanation. Reviews cited in the literature, including a 1997 trial in children with atopic dermatitis, found no benefit beyond placebo.[1]

chain: Device-based sessions aimed at allergies and inflammation
Practitioners say symptoms such as eczema ease
angle.text: Practitioners offer bioresonance for allergy and skin complaints, with the stated goal of calmer, clearer skin. This is the proponents' claim; the proposed mechanism has not been demonstrated.

infobox: US FDA: Class III where resistance-measuring devices diagnose or treat disease

paras: Devices vary, but practitioners describe a machine that picks up oscillations through electrodes, processes them, and returns modified signals through the same electrodes. Some machines include a circuit that measures skin resistance, similar to the Scientology E-meter.[1]

Franz Morell and his son-in-law, engineer Erich Rasche, invented the method in Germany in 1977 and marketed it as MORA-Therapie, combining the first syllables of their names.[1] It later spread under names including BICOM and bioresonance.

Practitioners claim the device can detect a range of diseases and addictions and treat disease without drugs by reversing the cellular changes that disease causes.[1] Clinics apply this to allergy, eczema and similar complaints that affect skin appearance.

Researchers classify the practice as pseudoscience because no explanation of how it could work has been offered.[1] Edzard Ernst and Ben Goldacre are among critics; Goldacre criticised the BBC for reporting a clinic's claim of a 70% smoking-cessation rate as fact.[1] WebMD states there is no reliable scientific evidence that it indicates disease or treats any condition, and Quackwatch has disputed its proposed mechanism.[1]

In the US, the FDA classifies devices that diagnose and treat disease using resistance measurements as Class III, requiring approval before marketing. It has banned some such devices and prosecuted sellers over false health claims; a 2002 case involved a 'BioResonance' promoter who settled charges.[1]
Studies cited in encyclopedic summaries include a 2005 review of unproven allergy diagnostics and a 1997 trial in children with atopic dermatitis, which found no effect beyond placebo.[1]

timeline.event: Morell and Rasche develop MORA therapy in Germany.[1]
Trial in children with atopic dermatitis reports no effect beyond placebo.[1]
A 'BioResonance' promoter settles US charges over claims.[1]
